title: MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition

Title:MARS: Training Multilingual Search Agents for Retriever-Free Evidence Acquisition
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Existing multilingual retrieval-augmented generation relies heavily on learned retrievers and similarity-based ranking from multilingual collections, which are vulnerable to cross-lingual retrieval errors and indexing overhead. In this paper, we explore retriever-free multilingual search, where the model directly interacts with raw corpora through executable shell commands. This paradigm shifts the bottleneck to multilingual search action generation, where exact search is sensitive to entity surface forms and outcome-only supervision provides limited guidance for multi-turn search. To address these challenges, we propose MARS, a multilingual search agent in direct corpus interaction (DCI) with reinforcement learning (RL). MARS introduces corpus-native entity grounding to recover reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence, mitigating failure to retrieve evidence. Meanwhile, we present a redundancy-aware search reward to encourage concise and effective search trajectories, addressing training collapse in RL of multilingual scenarios. Experiments show that \ours~consistently outperforms strong retrieval-based and DCI baselines, while demonstrating robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially reducing redundant corpus interactions.

report.summary: MARS trains multilingual search agents to query raw corpora directly via shell commands, using entity grounding and redundancy-aware RL to outperform retriever-based RAG.
report.background: Multilingual retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically depends on learned retrievers, multilingual embeddings, and vector indexes to find evidence before an LLM answers. This pipeline works well in high-resource settings but is brittle across languages: entity names, transliterations, and scripts can mismatch, causing cross-lingual retrieval errors, while indexing large multilingual corpora adds cost and operational overhead. A newer alternative, direct corpus interaction (DCI), lets an agent search raw files with executable shell commands such as grep, skipping the retriever entirely. That shifts the hard problem from ranking documents to generating good search actions over many turns. Multilingual DCI is especially difficult because exact-match search is sensitive to surface forms and outcome-only reinforcement learning gives sparse guidance. MARS addresses this gap by combining reinforcement learning with corpus-native entity grounding and a redundancy-aware reward, aiming to make retriever-free evidence acquisition more reliable and efficient across languages.
key_points: MARS removes the learned retriever and vector index from multilingual RAG. Instead, the model acts as a search agent that runs shell commands directly against raw corpora. This reduces indexing overhead and avoids errors introduced by multilingual similarity ranking, but it makes the agent responsible for composing exact, executable searches across languages.

The system adds corpus-native entity grounding. Because exact search depends on how names appear in the corpus—scripts, transliterations, spelling variants—MARS recovers reliable lexical anchors from corpus evidence. This helps the agent avoid failed searches and retrieve supporting passages even when the user's language and document language differ.

MARS uses reinforcement learning with a redundancy-aware search reward. Outcome-only rewards are sparse for multi-turn search, and multilingual RL can collapse. The reward encourages concise, effective trajectories and penalizes repeated or wasteful corpus interactions, improving both answer evidence and search efficiency.

Experiments report that MARS consistently beats strong retrieval-based and direct-corpus-interaction baselines. It also shows robust cross-lingual generalization and substantially fewer redundant corpus interactions, suggesting retriever-free multilingual search can be competitive while reducing dependence on multilingual embedding quality.
report.impact: For the AI industry, MARS signals a possible architectural shift in RAG: from vector-database-centric pipelines to agentic, tool-using systems that search raw corpora directly. That could lower indexing costs and reduce cross-lingual retrieval mismatch, but it also raises latency, sandboxing, access-control, and reproducibility concerns. Developers would need to build and evaluate shell-command agents, design reward functions, and handle multilingual entity normalization, while relying less on off-the-shelf multilingual retrievers. Regular users could see better answers over mixed-language document collections, with search traces that are easier to audit, and potentially fewer hallucinations when evidence is correctly grounded. The trade-off is that performance depends on agent policy quality and corpus accessibility; poorly designed rewards or unsafe shell access could make systems slower, noisier, or riskier to deploy.
report.tools: To follow this line, watch direct-corpus-interaction search agents and RL training stacks. Useful building blocks include ripgrep/fd for fast corpus-native search, sandboxed shell or container environments for safe command execution, and RL frameworks such as Hugging Face TRL or OpenRLHF for reward-driven agent training. For multilingual evaluation, consider benchmarks like MIRACL and MKQA, plus entity-linking resources for script and transliteration variants. Check the paper's arXiv page for code or data releases before reproducing results.
